description: The HEART Score stratifies risk of major adverse cardiac events (MACE) in patients with chest pain. Combined with AHA/ACC guidelines for acute coronary syndrome management.

inclusion: Adults presenting with chest pain or anginal equivalent
exclusion: STEMI on initial ECG (direct to cath lab)

decision_rules.evidence_text: STEMI requires immediate reperfusion therapy. Primary PCI is preferred if available within 90 minutes of first medical contact.

decision_rules.description: Chest pain with typical anginal features
decision_rules.evidence_text: Typical anginal chest pain has 3 characteristics: substernal, provoked by exertion, relieved by rest/nitroglycerin. Presence of all 3 indicates definite angina.

decision_rules.description: Chest pain radiating to arm, jaw, or neck
decision_rules.evidence_text: Radiation of chest pain to the left arm increases likelihood ratio for MI to 2.3. Radiation to right arm or both arms further increases likelihood.
Diaphoresis with chest pain increases likelihood ratio for MI to 2.0. Combination of sweating, nausea, and vomiting highly suggestive of inferior MI.
Troponin elevation above the 99th percentile with rise/fall pattern confirms acute myocardial injury. Serial testing at 0 and 3 hours recommended.

decision_rules.description: Atypical ACS symptoms in high-risk population

action.rationale: Atypical presentation common in elderly, diabetics, women

decision_rules.evidence_text: Up to 1/3 of MI patients present without chest pain, especially elderly, diabetic, and female patients. Dyspnea may be the only symptom (anginal equivalent).

heart_score.description: HEART Score for Major Cardiac Events

interpretation.0-3: Low risk (0.9-1.7% MACE) - Consider discharge with follow-up
interpretation.4-6: Intermediate risk (12-16.6% MACE) - Admit for observation
interpretation.7-10: High risk (50-65% MACE) - Early invasive management

clarifying_questions.question: Can you describe the chest pain? Is it pressure, squeezing, or sharp?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 能描述一下胸痛吗？是压迫感、挤压感还是刺痛？

clarifying_questions.question: Does the pain radiate to your arm, jaw, neck, or back?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 疼痛有没有放射到手臂、下巴、脖子或背部？

clarifying_questions.question: Are you sweating, feeling nauseous, or short of breath?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 有没有出汗、恶心或呼吸困难？

clarifying_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, high blood pressure, or a history of heart disease?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 您有糖尿病、高血压或心脏病史吗？

clarifying_questions.question: When did the pain start? Is it constant or does it come and go?
clarifying_questions.question_zh: 疼痛什么时候开始的？是持续的还是间歇性的？

text_chunks.title: HEART Score for Chest Pain Evaluation
text_chunks.content: The HEART Score stratifies chest pain patients into low, intermediate, and high risk for major adverse cardiac events (MACE). Components: History (0-2 points based on typicality), ECG (0-2 points), Age (0-2 points), Risk factors (0-2 points), Troponin (0-2 points). Score 0-3: Low risk (1.7% MACE), consider discharge. Score 4-6: Intermediate (16.6% MACE), admit for observation. Score 7-10: High risk (65% MACE), early invasive strategy.
text_chunks.source: HEART Score, Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care 2012

text_chunks.title: ACS Red Flags - Immediate Action Required
text_chunks.content: Red flags in chest pain requiring immediate cardiology evaluation: (1) ST elevation on ECG - activate cath lab, (2) Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock), (3) New heart failure symptoms, (4) Ventricular arrhythmias, (5) Ongoing severe chest pain unrelieved by nitroglycerin, (6) Positive troponin with typical symptoms. These findings indicate high-risk ACS requiring immediate intervention.

text_chunks.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome Spectrum
text_chunks.content: Acute coronary syndrome encompasses: (1) STEMI - complete coronary occlusion with ST elevation, requires emergent reperfusion, (2) NSTEMI - partial occlusion with troponin elevation but no ST elevation, requires urgent risk stratification, (3) Unstable Angina - threatened occlusion without troponin rise, requires observation and risk stratification. All share underlying pathophysiology of atherosclerotic plaque rupture with thrombosis.

text_chunks.title: Atypical ACS Presentations
text_chunks.content: Atypical ACS presentations occur in up to 1/3 of patients, especially: (1) Women - may present with fatigue, dyspnea, nausea without chest pain, (2) Elderly - confusion, weakness, dyspnea may predominate, (3) Diabetics - silent ischemia due to neuropathy, (4) Post-surgical patients - pain attribution error. Anginal equivalents include: dyspnea on exertion, epigastric discomfort, jaw or arm pain without chest pain, unexplained diaphoresis.
text_chunks.source: AHA Scientific Statement on Sex Differences in ACS

text_chunks.title: Initial ACS Management
text_chunks.content: Initial ACS management includes: (1) Aspirin 325mg chewed immediately, (2) ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, (3) Continuous monitoring, (4) IV access, (5) Oxygen if SpO2 < 90%, (6) Nitroglycerin for ongoing pain (avoid if hypotensive or RV infarct), (7) Morphine for refractory pain, (8) Serial troponins at 0 and 3 hours, (9) Anticoagulation (heparin) once diagnosis confirmed, (10) Beta-blocker if no contraindications. For STEMI, activate cath lab for primary PCI.
